The best camera for beach holidays in 2026 is the GoPro Hero 13 Black — it's waterproof to 10m without a case, shrugs off sand, and survives the kind of abuse that kills mirrorless cameras. If you want better low-light and a bigger sensor for sunset shots, the DJI Osmo Action 5 Pro is a very close second. I've tested both across beach trips in Bali, the Algarve, and Thailand, and this guide is everything I wish someone had told me before I killed my first compact camera with a single gust of sandy wind.

Beaches are the single most hostile environment most holiday cameras ever meet. Salt, sand, UV, and water attack from four directions at once — and yet the beach is also where the best holiday footage happens. Here's how to get the shots without sacrificing your gear.

Key Takeaways

  • GoPro Hero 13 Black is the safest all-round beach pick; DJI Action 5 Pro wins for image quality and battery life.
  • An Insta360 X4 on a selfie stick is the best beach vlogging setup — no aiming, no missed moments.
  • Harsh midday sun needs ND filters or high shutter discipline; shoot golden hour whenever you can.
  • Never change lenses or open battery doors on the sand — do it inside a bag, or back at the hotel.
  • Rinse every saltwater-exposed camera in fresh water the same day, every day.

Quick Answer: Best Beach Camera 2026

Buy the GoPro Hero 13 Black if you want one camera that handles swimming, surfing, sandcastles, and sunset cocktails without anxiety. It's waterproof to 10m naked, shoots gorgeous 5.3K video, and the HyperSmooth stabilization means you can hand it to a kid on a bodyboard and still get usable footage. Expect to pay around $350-$450 depending on bundles.

If your beach holiday is more snorkeling and sunset vlogging than wipeouts, the DJI Osmo Action 5 Pro (also around $350-$450) gives you a larger sensor, better dynamic range in harsh sun, and dramatically better battery life. For 360 beach vlogs where you'd rather enjoy the moment than frame it, the Insta360 X4 is the pick.

What the Beach Does to Cameras

On a beach in Bali last year I watched a tourist pull a lovely mirrorless camera out of a tote bag, and within twenty minutes a gust of wind had blown sand across the towel, the bag, and inevitably the camera's zoom ring. That grinding sound when he twisted it? That was the end of that lens. Beaches destroy cameras in four specific ways:

  • Sand: Gets into lens rings, buttons, card slots, and charging ports. One grain in a motorised zoom mechanism can be fatal. Salt-laden sand is also mildly abrasive and will scratch lens coatings if you wipe a dirty lens.
  • Saltwater: Far worse than fresh water. Salt is corrosive — it eats seals, corrodes charging contacts, and leaves residue on glass that bakes on in the sun. A splash you ignore today is a dead button in three months.
  • Sun and heat: A black camera body in direct midday sun can overheat and shut down mid-recording. UV also degrades rubber grips and port covers over a two-week trip.
  • Water (obviously): Waves are sneakier than pools. A camera rated waterproof to 10m handles a snorkel, but a wave hitting at speed drives water into any weakness in the seals.
Warning: "Waterproof" ratings assume still, fresh-ish water at modest pressure. Jumping into the sea with a camera, or taking it body-surfing, briefly exceeds the rated pressure. Keep action cams on a wrist leash and treat the depth rating as a snorkel limit, not a scuba licence.

Top Beach Camera Picks

1. GoPro Hero 13 Black — Best Overall Beach Camera

The Hero 13 is the camera I grab when I don't know what the day will bring. Waterproof to 10m without housing, it has survived being buried by a toddler, dropped off a paddleboard, and dunked in rock pools on my trips. The new magnetic mounting system is brilliant on the beach — snap it off a chest mount and onto a selfie grip in two seconds, with no fiddly thumbscrews covered in wet sand. The interchangeable lens mods (including an ND filter set) matter more at the beach than anywhere else; read my full GoPro Hero 13 review for the beach testing details. Battery life is its one weakness in 4K high-frame-rate modes, so pack a spare.

2. DJI Osmo Action 5 Pro — Best Image Quality in the Surf

The DJI Osmo Action 5 Pro has a larger 1/1.3-inch sensor than the GoPro, and you can see it: cleaner sunset footage, better dynamic range when the sun is blazing off the water, and less noise in shaded beach bars. It's waterproof to 20m without a case — double the GoPro — and the battery simply refuses to die; I regularly got through a full beach day on one cell. The front touchscreen makes selfie vlogging on a sun lounger genuinely easy. Downsides: fewer lens mods, and the RockSteady stabilization is a hair behind HyperSmooth for full-on surf action.

3. Insta360 X4 — Best for Beach Vlogs

The Insta360 X4 changed how I film beach days. Because it records everything in 360 degrees at up to 8K, you just hold the stick up and live your life — swimming, walking the shoreline, playing volleyball — and pick the best angles later in the app. The invisible selfie stick effect gives you drone-like follow shots of yourself walking along the water with zero effort. It's waterproof to 10m, and the invisible stick even works underwater in good light. The trade-off: 360 footage needs editing time, and the exposed dual lenses demand a rinse and careful wiping (blow the sand off first, never rub).

4. Your Phone (in a Pouch) — The Honest Budget Option

Modern flagship phones like the iPhone 16 Pro are water resistant and shoot excellent 4K, but "water resistant" is a lab rating against fresh water, and Apple and Samsung both exclude liquid damage from warranty. If the phone is your only camera, buy a quality IPX8 floating pouch for around $15-$25, test it with a tissue inside first, and keep the phone out of the midday sun to avoid heat shutdowns.

Beach Shooting Techniques

Tame the midday sun. Beach light between 11am and 3pm is brutal — harsh shadows, blown-out sand, squinting subjects. Your best tools are an ND filter (the GoPro's ND lens mod or screw-on NDs for the Action 5 Pro) to keep shutter speed near double your frame rate, and simply choosing to film people facing away from the sun with the sea behind them. Even easier: do your main filming before 10am and after 4pm, and nap through the bad light like the locals do.

Expose for the highlights. Bright sand and water reflections trick every auto-exposure into underexposing faces. Dial in +0.5 to +1.0 EV compensation when people are your subject, or lock exposure on a face before you hit record.

Get low and get wet. The most-liked beach clips in my edits are always the half-submerged split shots and the low angles at the waterline where waves wash over the lens. A floating hand grip makes these safe and easy. Lick-and-wipe the lens (seriously — saliva prevents droplets beading) or use an anti-fog, water-repellent coating on the lens cover.

Pro tip: Film your "beach walk" b-roll at 120fps. Slow-motion waves, footprints filling with water, and hair in the wind are the glue shots that make a holiday edit feel cinematic. Our waterproof camera buying guide has frame-rate recommendations per camera.

Sand & Salt Gear-Care Rules

These are the rules I follow religiously after ruining a compact camera in 2019:

  • Never open anything on the beach. Battery swaps, card changes, and lens changes happen inside a closed bag at minimum — ideally back in your room. Sand falls upward when you're crouching on a towel.
  • Keep a dedicated beach bag. Cameras go in a zip-lock or dry bag inside the beach bag. Wet swimsuits and sandy towels never share a compartment with electronics.
  • Rinse the same day. After any saltwater exposure, rinse the camera under a gentle fresh-water tap (low pressure, not a jet), paying attention to buttons and port covers, then dry with a microfiber cloth. Salt left overnight starts corroding contacts.
  • Blow, don't wipe, a sandy lens. A blower or even a firm breath gets grains off before the microfiber touches glass. Wiping dry sand is sanding your coating.
  • Silica gel in the camera bag. Beach humidity plus air-conditioned rooms equals condensation. A couple of silica packets keep the bag dry.
Warning: Check every port door and battery latch for sand grains before closing them. A single grain trapped in the gasket creates a leak path that a snorkel session will find.

One-Day Beach Shot List

Steal my standard beach-day structure — it guarantees an edit with a beginning, middle, and end:

  • 07:30 — Empty beach establishing shots at sunrise: shoreline pans, waves at 120fps, footprints.
  • 09:00 — Breakfast/coffee flat-lay on the table, sea defocused behind.
  • 10:30 — First swim: POV walk into the water, half-underwater split shot, snorkel pass over the shallows.
  • 12:00 — Put the camera away (harsh light) and shoot only a quick timelapse of the beach filling up.
  • 15:00 — Activities: paddleboard follow-cam, beach volleyball at 120fps, kids' sandcastle hyperlapse.
  • 18:30 — Golden hour portraits at the waterline, silhouettes against the sunset, walking-away shot.
  • 20:00 — Beach bar/closing shot: cocktail cheers, string lights, wave sounds for the outro.

If you love this kind of location-driven filming structure, our City Through the Lens series applies the same one-day shot-list philosophy to cities around the world — it's a great companion read before any trip. Frequently Asked Questions

Is the GoPro Hero 13 waterproof enough for snorkeling?

Yes. The GoPro Hero 13 Black is waterproof to 10m (33ft) without any housing, which covers recreational snorkeling easily. For scuba diving below 10m you need GoPro's protective housing, rated to 60m. Always rinse it in fresh water after saltwater use.

How do I protect my camera from sand at the beach?

Keep the camera in a zip-lock or dry bag whenever you're not shooting, never open battery or card doors on the sand, and blow grains off the lens before wiping with microfiber. Do all battery and card swaps indoors or inside a closed bag.

Do I need an ND filter for beach video?

Strongly recommended. Bright sand and sea force very high shutter speeds that make video look jittery. An ND filter (or the GoPro Hero 13's ND lens mod) lets you keep shutter speed at roughly double your frame rate, which gives natural-looking motion even in harsh midday sun.

Action camera or phone for a beach holiday?

An action camera is the safer choice: it's truly waterproof, mounts anywhere, and a broken $400 GoPro hurts less than a drowned $1,200 phone. Use your phone for dry land shots and sunsets, and let the action cam handle everything wet and sandy.
